\title{Physically Verified Counterfactual Gating for Robust Cooperative LiDAR Perception: A Pre-registered Evaluation\\

\begin{abstract}
Intermediate-fusion cooperative perception lets a malicious sender spoof, remove or shift objects in the
receiver's output by editing the features it transmits. We study a defense that asks, per sender and per
6.4\,m tile, \emph{what changes if this sender is removed here?}, and switches a contribution off only when
the receiver's own LiDAR rays resolvably contradict the change (R1); regions the receiver cannot see are left
untouched. We evaluate R1 against a receiver-only box-level free-space filter (B-RAY), a feature-magnitude
check (B-NORM), ego-only perception and no defense in a pre-registered, one-time final test on
\TestScenarios{} OPV2V test scenarios (\TestFrames{} frames) under \NumConditions{} conditions, including
white-box PGD and B-NORM-aware stealth PGD feature attacks. The pre-registered primary, B-RAY, passes its
success rule under both AP definitions, narrowly under global-ranking AP (\VGlobBRAYDelta\pts, one-sided
$p=\VGlobBRAYP$ after Holm; two-sided CI \VGlobBRAYCI). R1 is the only defense whose effect is positive in all
\NumConditions{} conditions under global-ranking AP, and the only one that recovers removal attacks
(\dGlobPgdRemStStrongRONE\pts{} at the strongest level). Free-space filtering and the norm check fail against
optimized and stealthy attacks. The comparison of R1 with B-RAY reverses when OPV2V's default frame-order AP
is used (\VGlobRmB{} vs.\ \VFrameRmB\pts), a warning for evaluation practice in the field. A secondary,
held-out run of the frozen code on OPV2V's Culver City split (simulated, real-city layout, unseen during detector
training and during all MINT development; \CulFrames{} frames) reproduces the signs of the test effects (R1
\CulHeadGlobRONE, B-RAY \CulHeadGlobBRAY\pts{} under global-ranking AP), but B-RAY's gain is not significant
there. We report the
costs: receiver-blind regions stay undefended, R1 switches off useful contributions on clean frames, and its
compute overhead grows with the number of cars.
\end{abstract}

\begin{IEEEkeywords}
cooperative perception, V2V, adversarial robustness, LiDAR, free-space verification, counterfactual,
pre-registration, average precision
\end{IEEEkeywords}

%======================================================================
\section{Introduction}
%======================================================================
Cooperative perception (CP) lets connected vehicles share what they sense. In \emph{intermediate fusion},
each sender encodes its LiDAR scan into a bird's-eye-view (BEV) feature map, and the receiver fuses the maps
and decodes 3D boxes~\cite{xu2022opv2v,hu2022where2comm,xu2022v2xvit}. The receiver cannot check a feature
map directly, so an insider can perturb what it sends and make the receiver see a car that is not there,
miss one that is, or misplace
one~\cite{tu2021adversarial,zhang2024cad,wang2025lucia,zhang2026poseguard}.

Defenses fall into three groups. \emph{Consensus and counterfactual} defenses compare outputs with and
without a sender and reject whole agents~\cite{li2023robosac,zhao2024made,hu2025cpguard,tao2026gcp}.
\emph{Free-space} defenses test detected boxes against LiDAR physics~\cite{sun2020carlo,hau2021shadowcatcher,zhang2024cad}.
\emph{Anomaly} defenses test feature statistics~\cite{zhang2026latentguardian}. Agent-level rejection
discards a sender's useful information everywhere to stop an attack that is usually local. Box-level
free-space checks can only delete boxes, so they cannot restore a removed object.

We combine the two ideas at a finer grain. R1 attributes each change in the receiver's output to one sender
in one 6.4\,m tile by decoding with and without that sender. It then tests the change (an added, removed or
shifted box) against the receiver's own LiDAR rays with a Wilson-95 resolvability margin. A contribution is
switched off only where the receiver can see and the evidence is resolvable; everything else is kept.
To our knowledge, this tile-level, physically verified counterfactual has not been evaluated before; the ray
check itself is not new~\cite{sun2020carlo,zhang2024cad}.

We report the evaluation as it was pre-registered, including the parts that did not favour R1. The primary
method of the final test is \emph{B-RAY}, a box-level receiver-ray filter. It was chosen over R1 by a rule
fixed before seeing development block~H results (decision D-57); R1 became the key secondary. All analyses,
thresholds and attack levels were frozen before the test data were opened, and the test was run once.

\textbf{Contributions.}
\begin{enumerate}
\item R1, a tile-level counterfactual defense whose ADD/REMOVE/SHIFT effects are verified against the receiver's
own rays, with UNKNOWN$=$keep (Sec.~\ref{sec:method}).
\item A pre-registered, one-time final test on \TestScenarios{} OPV2V test scenarios (\TestFrames{} frames) with
\NumConditions{} conditions, including copy-paste, point-level, receiver-blind, PGD and B-NORM-aware stealth PGD
attacks, against re-implemented baselines (Sec.~\ref{sec:protocol}), and a secondary, held-out domain-shift
evaluation of the frozen code on OPV2V's unseen Culver City town (simulated sensor; Sec.~\ref{sec:culver}).
\item The finding that the pre-registered primary (B-RAY) passes narrowly. R1 is the only defense positive in
all conditions under global-ranking AP, and the only one that recovers removal attacks
(\dGlobPgdRemStStrongRONE\pts{} at the strongest level). Free-space filters and norm checks fail against
optimized or stealthy attacks (Sec.~\ref{sec:results}).
\item The finding that OPV2V's default frame-order AP reverses the R1-vs-B-RAY conclusion, a methodological
warning for the field (Sec.~\ref{sec:apflip}).
\item Measured limits: receiver-blind regions, a single attacker, CARLA sensor realism, and compute overhead
that grows with the number of cars (Secs.~\ref{sec:runtime},~\ref{sec:discussion}).
\end{enumerate}

%======================================================================
\section{Related Work}
%======================================================================
\textbf{Attacks on cooperative perception.}
Tu et al.~\cite{tu2021adversarial} perturb a sender's intermediate message with gradient attacks, the
template for most later work. Zhang et al.~\cite{zhang2024cad} fabricate occlusion-consistent points by ray
casting and run online PGD on features, for spoofing and removal. SOMBRA~\cite{wang2025lucia} hijacks
AttFuse's per-pixel attention on OPV2V to remove objects. PosePert~\cite{zhang2026poseguard} shifts existing
objects by small amounts. The Blind Area Confusion attack~\cite{tao2026gcp} concentrates perturbations where
the victim cannot see, and MVIG~\cite{tao2026mvig} optimizes attack placement against consensus defenses.
TrustFlip~\cite{liu2026trustflip} turns trust-based defenses against benign vehicles. Physical spoofing of the
victim's own LiDAR~\cite{cao2019advlidar} breaks any defense that trusts the receiver's sensor, including ours.

\textbf{Consensus and counterfactual defenses.}
ROBOSAC~\cite{li2023robosac} samples sender subsets until the fused result agrees with ego-only perception.
MADE~\cite{zhao2024made} tests each agent with a match loss between outputs with and without that agent and
a reconstruction loss, using conformal p-values and Benjamini--Hochberg control~\cite{benjamini1995fdr}.
CP-Guard~\cite{hu2025cpguard} and GCP~\cite{tao2026gcp} detect malicious agents by consensus, GCP adding
spatial--temporal cues. GLST~\cite{he2026glst} addresses stealthy multi-attacker feature injection. LUCIA~\cite{wang2025lucia}
scales attention by per-agent trust, and MATE~\cite{hallyburton2025mate} maintains Beta trust over agents and tracks.
All of these decide per agent (or per subset or track). R1 uses the same with/without-sender question as
MADE and ROBOSAC, but decides per sender and tile, and accepts a decision only when the receiver's own rays
resolve it.

\textbf{Free-space defenses.}
CARLO~\cite{sun2020carlo} checks single-vehicle boxes for laser penetration and free space;
Shadow-Catcher~\cite{hau2021shadowcatcher} checks for the LiDAR shadow a real object must cast. CAD~\cite{zhang2024cad}
shares occupancy maps between vehicles and runs free-space checks on the fused result, with a local-only
variant. Our B-RAY baseline is a receiver-only box-level check in this style, with a Wilson margin; we claim
no novelty for it.

\textbf{Anomaly defenses.}
Latent Guardian~\cite{zhang2026latentguardian} compares collaborator and ego features by structure,
direction and energy. B-NORM is the simplest member of this family: a per-scale magnitude-ratio threshold.

\textbf{Evaluation practice.}
OPV2V and OpenCOOD~\cite{xu2022opv2v} are the standard benchmark for AttFuse-style intermediate fusion;
V2V4Real~\cite{xu2023v2v4real} and Mixed Signals~\cite{luo2025mixedsignals} provide real data.
Adaptive-attack guidance~\cite{carlini2019evaluating,tramer2020adaptive} asks that defenses be tested against
attackers who know them, which motivates our stealth PGD. AP is usually computed by ranking detections by score
across the whole set, as in PASCAL VOC~\cite{everingham2010voc}; OpenCOOD's default instead accumulates true and false positives
frame by frame. We are not aware of prior CP work that reports both. Pre-registration~\cite{nosek2018preregistration} is rare
in this field.

%======================================================================
\section{Threat Model and Problem Setup}
\label{sec:threat}
%======================================================================
\textbf{System.} A receiver (agent~0) and senders $1,\dots,n{-}1$ ($n\le 5$ on the test set) run AttFuse
PointPillars~\cite{xu2022opv2v,lang2019pointpillars} with the released OPV2V checkpoint, unchanged. Following
OpenCOOD's convention, senders project their points into the receiver's LiDAR frame before encoding, so
sender features $f_{i,k}$ at scale $k\in\{1,2,3\}$ arrive on the receiver's BEV grid. The receiver fuses
them with per-pixel attention and decodes boxes $Y^{+}$ (Fig.~\ref{fig:pipeline}).

\textbf{Attacker.} One insider, always sender~1, controls only what it transmits: its features at all three
scales (feature attacks) or its points before encoding (point attack). For PGD the attacker is white-box:
it knows the weights, the receiver's features, the fusion and the heads. It does not control the receiver's
sensor, pose or software, and it does not collude with others. Frames with $n=1$ have no sender and are
scored as clean.

\textbf{Defender.} The receiver trusts only its own LiDAR scan and pose. It may decode received features
any number of times (receiver-side computation). It never uses ground truth at inference.

\textbf{Goal.} Maximize AP@0.7 for cars on attacked frames while losing as little as possible on clean
frames. A defense may delete boxes (B-RAY), drop senders (B-NORM, ego-only) or switch off a sender in a tile
(R1).

\subsection{Counterfactual effects}
Let $Y^{+}$ be the receiver's boxes decoded from all agents and $Y^{-}(i)$ the boxes decoded with sender
$i$ excluded:
\begin{equation}
Y^{+}=\mathrm{Dec}\big(\mathrm{Fuse}(f_0,f_1,\dots,f_{n-1})\big),\quad
Y^{-}(i)=\mathrm{Dec}\big(\mathrm{Fuse}(\{f_j\}_{j\neq i})\big).
\label{eq:cf}
\end{equation}
We match $Y^{+}$ and $Y^{-}(i)$ by Hungarian assignment on BEV IoU (match if IoU $\ge 0.1$) and define the
effects of sender $i$:
\begin{equation}
\begin{aligned}
\mathrm{ADD}_i &= \{b\in Y^{+} : b \text{ unmatched in } Y^{-}(i)\},\\
\mathrm{REMOVE}_i &= \{b\in Y^{-}(i) : b \text{ unmatched in } Y^{+}\},\\
\mathrm{SHIFT}_i &= \{(b^{+},b^{-}) \text{ matched}: \|c^{+}-c^{-}\|>0.3\,\text{m} \lor |\Delta\psi|>10^\circ\},
\end{aligned}
\label{eq:effects}
\end{equation}
with $c$ the BEV box centre and $\psi$ the heading. Each effect belongs to the 6.4\,m tile $u$ that contains
its box centre (in either version for SHIFT). The \emph{unit} of decision is the pair $(i,u)$.

\subsection{Receiver ray evidence}
For a box $b$, each return of the receiver's own scan defines a ray from the receiver's sensor. A ray that
ends inside $b$ is \emph{support} (SUP); one that passes through $b$ and ends behind it is \emph{traversal}
(TRAV); one that ends before $b$ carries no information. Rays without a return are never counted as
traversal. The support ratio is
\begin{equation}
s(b)=\frac{\mathrm{SUP}(b)}{\mathrm{SUP}(b)+\mathrm{TRAV}(b)}.
\label{eq:s}
\end{equation}
An effect is KNOWN if every box it involves has $N=\mathrm{SUP}+\mathrm{TRAV}\ge 3$ and is not the receiver's
own box; otherwise the unit is UNKNOWN.

\subsection{Resolvability gate (R1)}
For $k$ supporting rays out of $N$, the Wilson score interval~\cite{wilson1927} with $z=1.96$ is
\begin{equation}
\mathrm{lo},\mathrm{hi}=\frac{k+z^2/2}{N+z^2}\mp\frac{z}{N+z^2}\sqrt{\frac{k(N-k)}{N}+\frac{z^2}{4}}.
\label{eq:wilson}
\end{equation}
Rays through one box are spatially correlated, so this is a \emph{resolvability margin} on counts, not a
probability. Each KNOWN effect receives a verdict, with $s^{+}$ ($s^{-}$) the ratio of its box in $Y^{+}$
($Y^{-}(i)$):
\begin{equation}
\begin{aligned}
\text{ADD:}\ &\text{gate iff } \mathrm{hi}(s^{+})<0.5, &&\text{useful iff } \mathrm{lo}(s^{+})>0.5,\\
\text{REMOVE:}\ &\text{gate iff } \mathrm{lo}(s^{-})>0.5, &&\text{useful iff } \mathrm{hi}(s^{-})<0.5,\\
\text{SHIFT:}\ &\text{gate iff } I^{+}\cap I^{-}=\emptyset \land s^{+}<s^{-}, &&\text{useful iff } I^{+}\cap I^{-}=\emptyset \land s^{+}>s^{-},
\end{aligned}
\label{eq:gate}
\end{equation}
where $I^{\pm}$ are the Wilson intervals. The ``useful'' conditions mirror the gate conditions: an effect the
rays resolvably confirm protects its unit.

\subsection{Tile gating and composed output}
A unit is gated iff it is KNOWN, at least one of its effects gates, and none is resolvably useful:
\begin{equation}
g_{i,u}=\mathbb{1}[\text{KNOWN}_{i,u}]\cdot\mathbb{1}[\exists e:\text{gate}(e)]\cdot\mathbb{1}[\nexists e:\text{useful}(e)].
\label{eq:unitgate}
\end{equation}
UNKNOWN units are kept. With $S_u=\{i: g_{i,u}=1\}$, the output is composed tile by tile from decodes without
the gated senders,
\begin{equation}
Y_{\mathrm{R1}}=\bigcup_{u} \big\{\,b\in Y^{-}(S_u) : b \text{ centred in } u\,\big\},\qquad Y^{-}(\emptyset)=Y^{+},
\label{eq:compose}
\end{equation}
re-using the decodes of~\eqref{eq:cf} and decoding again only for tiles that gate two or more senders.
Composition was checked against a direct masked decode on every test scenario (all identical). R1 has no
tunable threshold. The ablation \emph{R1-noREMOVE} never lets a REMOVE verdict gate (its mirror condition is
kept).

\subsection{Baselines}
\textbf{B-RAY} (pre-registered primary) applies R1's ADD test to the final boxes without any counterfactual:
\begin{equation}
Y_{\mathrm{B\text{-}RAY}}=\{\,b\in Y^{+} : \lnot\big(\text{KNOWN}(b)\land \mathrm{hi}(s(b))<0.5\big)\}.
\label{eq:bray}
\end{equation}
It is a receiver-only free-space filter in the style of CARLO's penetration check and CAD's local-only
variant~\cite{sun2020carlo,zhang2024cad}. It can only delete boxes. Because of the Wilson margin, a box needs at
least four traversing rays and no support to be deleted.

\textbf{B-NORM} drops sender $i$ for the whole frame if, at any scale $k$,
$\overline{|f_{i,k}|}/\overline{|f_{0,k}|}>\tau_k$, with $\tau_k$ the 99.5th percentile of this ratio over clean
development frames (block~H; $\tau_1=\BnormTauOne$, $\tau_3=\BnormTauThree$). \textbf{Ego-only} drops all
senders. All baselines are parameter-free at test time.

\subsection{Ground-truth harm labels (evaluation only)}
To audit what R1 switches off, we label each unit offline with ground truth. With
$L_u(Y)=\#\mathrm{FP}+\#\mathrm{FN}+0.5\sum_{\mathrm{TP}}(1-\mathrm{IoU})$ over boxes centred in tile $u$
(Hungarian matching at BEV IoU $\ge 0.5$),
\begin{equation}
D_{i,u}=L_u(Y^{+})-L_u\big(Y^{-}(i,u)\big),\quad
\begin{cases}\text{HARMFUL} & D>0.5\\ \text{USEFUL} & D<-0.5\\ \text{NEUTRAL} & \text{otherwise.}\end{cases}
\label{eq:harm}
\end{equation}
Gating a USEFUL unit is a \emph{false switch-off}. The labels are never used by any defense.

\section{Experimental Protocol}
\label{sec:protocol}
%======================================================================
\subsection{Data and exposure}
We use OPV2V~\cite{xu2022opv2v} with the released AttFuse checkpoint on CPU. Table~\ref{tab:splits} lists the
three blocks. Block~T was used to write R1. Block~H was a held-out check of the frozen R1 (E4); after that it
was exposed, and the primary selection and the stealth attacks were developed on it. The test block is the
OPV2V test split minus one scenario that had been opened earlier: \TestScenarios{} scenarios, \TestFrames{}
frames, with $n=1$ in \TestNOne{} frames, $n=2$ in \TestNTwo, $n=3$ in \TestNThree{} and $n\ge 4$ in
\TestNFourPlus. Before the test, only clean detector outputs on it had been seen. Culver City was not used in
the test. After it, the frozen code was run once on OPV2V's Culver City split as a separate, secondary
held-out domain-shift evaluation (Sec.~\ref{sec:culver}).
\textbf{All block~T and H numbers in this paper are development numbers} and are never pooled with test
numbers.

\subsection{Pre-registration history}
Every rule was committed before the data it governs were opened. The original pre-registration (v1) made R1
the primary. Before any B-RAY result on block~H existed, we fixed rule D-57: if the block-H 95\% CI of
R1~$-$~B-RAY (frame-order AP, 10-frame bootstrap) had its lower bound above zero, R1 would stay primary;
otherwise B-RAY would become primary and R1 the key secondary. On H the difference was negative
(\DevHFrameRmB\pts{} \dev), so B-RAY became the primary (D-58). Pre-registration v2 added a Holm co-test of
B-RAY and R1 against no defense. A pre-test audit then found that the sign of R1~$-$~B-RAY on H depends on the
AP definition (Table~\ref{tab:devtest}). Rather than switch the primary a second time, v3 (D-64) requires the
v2 success rule to pass under \emph{both} AP definitions, quotes headline numbers in global-ranking AP, and
reports ``AP-definition-dependent'' where the two disagree. v3 also added B-NORM and the PGD conditions as
secondary conditions (D-65--D-68). v3.1 (D-70) added two strong stealth levels ($r=1.0$, marked $\dagger$)
\textbf{after seeing development results on H}; they are never used for a criterion. v3.2 (D-71) fixed a
bug in the stream code that crashed the first attempt before any result was written; no method, condition or
criterion changed.

\subsection{Attack conditions}
Table~\ref{tab:attacks} lists the \NumConditions{} conditions. The copy-paste families (spoof, remove, shift)
edit 3.2\,m-aligned patches of the attacker's feature maps at random locations; \emph{spoof (points)} copies a
car's points to an empty spot and re-encodes; \emph{spoof, receiver-blind} places the spoof only where the
receiver has fewer than three rays (a visibility-aware attacker). An attack is \emph{applied} when it can be
placed and \emph{realized} when it changes the undefended output; unapplied frames are scored as clean.

\textbf{PGD.} The attacker perturbs its features at all scales within $\|\delta_k\|_\infty\le\epsilon_k=r\,\sigma_k$,
with $\sigma_k$ the standard deviation of clean sender features on block~H. With step $\eta_k=\epsilon_k/4$, 10
sign-gradient ascent steps~\cite{madry2018pgd} and a uniform random start,
\begin{equation}
\delta_k^{t+1}=\Pi_{\mathcal{B}_k}\!\Big(\delta_k^{t}+\eta_k\,\mathrm{sign}\big(\nabla_{\delta_k}\mathcal{L}(\delta^{t})\big)\Big),
\label{eq:pgd}
\end{equation}
where $\mathcal{B}_k=\{\delta:|\delta|\le\epsilon_k,\ f_{1,k}+\delta\ge 0\}$. The loss uses the clean fused output as
pseudo-labels (no ground truth): \emph{untargeted} maximizes classification and regression loss on all anchors;
\emph{remove} minimizes the scores of the clean boxes. Plain PGD at the level selected on H ($r=0.25$) is caught
by B-NORM on every frame (Sec.~\ref{sec:pgd}). The \textbf{stealth} variants add B-NORM's constraint after every
step, via the exact Euclidean projection onto the box and a mean-magnitude bound:
\begin{equation}
\begin{aligned}
\delta_k &\leftarrow \mathrm{clip}\big(\delta_k-\lambda_k,\ \ell_k,\ \epsilon_k\big),\quad \ell_k=\max(-\epsilon_k,-f_{1,k}),\\
\lambda_k &= \min\Big\{\lambda\ge 0:\ \overline{f_{1,k}+\mathrm{clip}(\delta_k-\lambda,\ell_k,\epsilon_k)}\le 0.95\,\tau_k\,\overline{|f_{0,k}|}\Big\}.
\end{aligned}
\label{eq:stealth}
\end{equation}
$\lambda_k$ is found by bisection. Frames where the constraint has no solution are not attacked (``stealth
infeasible'', scored as clean): \InfeasiblePgdUntSt, \InfeasiblePgdRemSt, \InfeasiblePgdUntStStrong{} and
\InfeasiblePgdRemStStrong{} of \WithSenderPgdRemSt{} sender frames for the four stealth conditions.

\subsection{Metrics}
$\Delta$AP@0.7 is the AP@0.7 of a defense minus that of no defense on the same frames, in AP points. The
attack loss is $L=\mathrm{AP}(\text{clean, none})-\mathrm{AP}(\text{attacked, none})$, and
\begin{equation}
\mathrm{Rec}=\Delta\mathrm{AP}/L\ \ (\text{n/a if }L<0.005),\qquad
\mathrm{CleanLoss}=1-\frac{\mathrm{AP}(m,\text{clean})}{\mathrm{AP}(\text{none},\text{clean})}.
\label{eq:rec}
\end{equation}
\textbf{Two AP definitions.} Let detections $j$ carry a score $c_j$, a frame index $t_j$ and a true-positive
flag $\mathrm{tp}_j$ (IoU $\ge 0.7$), and let $G$ be the number of ground-truth cars. For an ordering $\pi$,
\begin{equation}
p_k=\frac{1}{k}\sum_{j\le k}\mathrm{tp}_{\pi(j)},\quad r_k=\frac{1}{G}\sum_{j\le k}\mathrm{tp}_{\pi(j)},\quad
\mathrm{AP}_\pi=\sum_k (r_k-r_{k-1})\max_{k'\ge k}p_{k'}.
\label{eq:ap}
\end{equation}
\emph{Global-ranking AP} uses $\pi_G$, all detections sorted by descending $c_j$. \emph{Frame-order AP}, the
OpenCOOD default used in OPV2V papers, uses $\pi_F$, which concatenates detections frame by frame in order of
$t_j$. Under $\pi_F$, a false positive in an early frame lowers the precision of every later detection,
whatever its score. Our NumPy implementation matches OpenCOOD's to $\NumpyOpencoodDiff$.

\subsection{Statistics}
Primary CIs come from a scenario bootstrap~\cite{efron1979bootstrap} (15 clusters, $B=\BootB$ resamples, seed 0); a 10-frame block bootstrap
stratified by scenario is reported as secondary. For a statistic $\theta$ with bootstrap replicates $\theta^*_b$,
\begin{equation}
p=\frac{1+\#\{b:\theta^*_b\le 0\}}{B+1}.
\label{eq:p}
\end{equation}
B-RAY and R1 are co-tested against no defense with Holm's step-down procedure~\cite{holm1979} at $\alpha=0.05$
within each AP definition: with $p_{(1)}\le p_{(2)}$, reject $H_{(1)}$ if $p_{(1)}\le\alpha/2$, then $H_{(2)}$ if
also $p_{(2)}\le\alpha$. The pre-registered success rule (v2) requires B-RAY to be Holm-rejected on the mean
$\Delta$AP@0.7 over the four original attacks (spoof, remove, shift by feature; spoof by points) \emph{and} the
upper scenario-CI bound of B-RAY's clean loss to be at most 1\%, under both AP definitions. The key secondary,
R1~$-$~B-RAY, is a paired difference whose scenario CI selects one of three pre-written statements.

\subsection{Pre-registered verdict}
\textbf{The primary passes under both AP definitions} (Table~\ref{tab:verdict}). Under global-ranking AP,
B-RAY improves the mean of the four original attacks by \VGlobBRAYDelta\pts; the one-sided bootstrap test rejects
after Holm ($p=\VGlobBRAYP$, threshold \VGlobBRAYHolmThr), but the two-sided 95\% scenario CI
\VGlobBRAYCI\pts{} includes zero. The pass is narrow. Under frame-order AP the gain is \VFrameBRAYDelta\pts{}
\VFrameBRAYCI{} ($p=\VFrameBRAYP$). B-RAY's clean loss stays inside the 1\% bound under both definitions.

R1, the co-tested key secondary, gains \VGlobRONEDelta\pts{} \VGlobRONECI{} under global-ranking AP ($p=\VGlobRONEP$,
rejected) and \VFrameRONEDelta\pts{} \VFrameRONECI{} under frame-order AP ($p=\VFrameRONEP$, not rejected).
The key secondary R1~$-$~B-RAY is \textbf{AP-definition-dependent}: \VGlobRmB\pts{} \VGlobRmBCI{} under
global-ranking AP, for which the pre-registered statement reads ``\VGlobRmBStatement'', and \VFrameRmB\pts{}
\VFrameRmBCI{} under frame-order AP: ``\VFrameRmBStatement''.

\subsection{Every condition}

Under global-ranking AP, \textbf{R1 is the only defense whose CI lies above zero in all \NumConditions{}

feature spoofs), but its effect is zero or negative on removals (\dGlobRemoveFeatBRAY, \dGlobPgdRemBRAY\pts{} on

ego-only also helps (\dGlobPgdRemStStrongEgo\pts), because the attack does more damage than losing cooperation.
The ablation R1-noREMOVE behaves like B-RAY on removals (\dGlobPgdRemStStrongRNoRem\pts{} at the strong level),
so the REMOVE test is what recovers removed objects.

Under frame-order AP the picture changes. B-RAY's gains on spoofing grow (\dFrameSpoofFeatBRAY\pts{} on feature
spoofs) and it gains \dFramePgdUntStStrongBRAY\pts{} \ciFramePgdUntStStrongBRAY{} on strong untargeted stealth
PGD$^\dagger$, while R1 loses on clean frames (\dFrameCleanRONE\pts{} \ciFrameCleanRONE) and its CIs include zero
on most attacks.

\subsection{Optimized and stealthy attacks}
\label{sec:pgd}
Plain PGD is trivially caught: B-NORM flags the attacker on \CatchPgdUnt{} of frames at $r=0.25$. Catching costs
as much as ego-only, so B-NORM lowers AP (\dGlobPgdUntBNORM\pts{} on untargeted PGD). The B-NORM-aware stealth
attacks drive its catch rate to \CatchPgdUntSt{} at every level (Fig.~\ref{fig:bnorm}), while the stealth
removal attack still costs \LossGlobPgdRemSt\pts{} at $r=0.25$ and \LossGlobPgdRemStStrong\pts{} at $r=1.0^\dagger$.
B-RAY's recovery of PGD attacks is at most \RecGlobPgdUntStStrongBRAY{} under global-ranking AP and
\RecFramePgdUntStStrongBRAY{} under frame-order AP (Fig.~\ref{fig:pgdrec}). R1 recovers \RecGlobPgdRemRONE{}
of plain and \RecGlobPgdRemStRONE{} of stealth PGD removal at $r=0.25$, and \RecGlobPgdRemStStrongRONE{} at the
strong level (global-ranking AP). Against untargeted PGD all defenses recover little (R1 at most
\RecGlobPgdUntStRONE).

The expectations written before any PGD run were checked descriptively. ``B-RAY recovery $<0.10$ under both AP
definitions'' held in five of six PGD conditions and failed on strong untargeted stealth PGD$^\dagger$
(frame-order recovery \RecFramePgdUntStStrongBRAY). ``R1's CI above zero under both definitions'' on removal
held only at the strong level$^\dagger$; at $r=0.25$ the frame-order CIs include zero. ``B-NORM catch
$\le 5\%$'' held for all stealth conditions.

\subsection{R1 versus B-RAY, and the AP-definition flip}
\label{sec:apflip}
Fig.~\ref{fig:rmb} shows the paired difference per condition. Under global-ranking AP, R1 is better on the
pre-registered mean (\VGlobRmB\pts{} \VGlobRmBCI) and on removals (\RmBGlobPgdRemSt\pts{} \RmBGlobPgdRemStCI{} on
stealth PGD removal). Under frame-order AP, R1 is worse (\VFrameRmB\pts{} \VFrameRmBCI). The same flip appeared
on development block~H (Table~\ref{tab:devtest}) and is why the primary is B-RAY: D-57 compared the two under
frame-order AP. The two metrics differ in how a low-score false positive is charged. Global ranking puts it at
the tail of the precision--recall curve, where it costs little. Frame-order accumulation charges it at the
position of its frame, lowering precision for every later frame. Deleting low-score fakes, which B-RAY does,
therefore earns more under frame-order AP, and so does the attack loss of a spoof (e.g.\ \LossFrameSpoofFeat{}
vs.\ \LossGlobSpoofFeat\pts{} for feature spoofs). R1's false switch-offs on clean frames are charged the same
way. \textbf{A ranking between CP defenses can thus depend on an evaluation flag that OPV2V papers rarely state.}

\subsection{Unseen-town evaluation (Culver City)}
\label{sec:culver}
After the test, we ran the frozen code once on OPV2V's Culver City split (\CulScenarios{} scenarios,
\CulFrames{} frames, $n=\CulNmin$--\CulNmax). This is a secondary, held-out domain-shift evaluation, planned and
committed before any Culver City data were downloaded (D-72). The town is simulated with the same CARLA LiDAR
model as the rest of OPV2V, but its layout is modelled on the real Culver City, and it was unseen during
detector training and during all MINT development. \textbf{It is not real-sensor data.} Methods, $\sigma_k$,
$\tau_k$, attack levels, seeds and analysis were reused unchanged; nothing was fitted on Culver City. A planned
check on the first scenario, before any defense or attack ran, gave clean AP@0.7 of \CulSanityAP{} (frame
order, \CulSanityFrames{} frames). Over all scenarios, the no-defense frame-order AP@0.7 is \CulAPCleanFrame{}
(\CulPublishedAP{} released with the checkpoint~\cite{xu2022opv2v}). Table~\ref{tab:culver} sets the headline
numbers next to the test. The two are never pooled, and with four scenarios the scenario CIs are coarse.

Under global-ranking AP, R1's mean gain over the four original attacks is \CulHeadGlobRONE\pts{}
\CulHeadGlobRONECI{} (Holm reject). B-RAY's is \CulHeadGlobBRAY\pts{} \CulHeadGlobBRAYCI{} ($p=\CulVGlobBRAYP$,
not rejected). The v3.2 success rule, applied descriptively, therefore \CulVGlobPass{} under global-ranking AP
and \CulVFramePass{} under frame-order AP (B-RAY \CulHeadFrameBRAY, R1 \CulHeadFrameRONE\pts; both rejected).
Clean cost stays below 1\% for both. R1~$-$~B-RAY is \CulVGlobRmB\pts{} \CulVGlobRmBCI{} under global ranking
and \CulVFrameRmB\pts{} \CulVFrameRmBCI{} under frame order. That is the sign pattern of the test, but the
frame-order difference is not resolved. On the strong stealth removal ($r=1.0^\dagger$), R1 recovers
\CulDGlobPgdRemStStrongRONE{} of \CulLossGlobPgdRemStStrong\pts{} (recovery \CulRecGlobPgdRemStStrongRONE; test
\RecGlobPgdRemStStrongRONE) and B-RAY \CulDGlobPgdRemStStrongBRAY\pts. B-NORM catches \CulCatchPgdUnt{} of plain
PGD and \CulCatchPgdRemStStrong{} of strong stealth PGD, and flags \CulCatchClean{} of clean frames (test
\CatchClean). No defense recovers the receiver-blind spoof. The direction of every headline effect transfers
to the unseen town. B-RAY's small global-ranking gain does not reach significance on four scenarios.

%======================================================================
\section{Discussion and Limitations}
\label{sec:discussion}
%======================================================================
\textbf{Receiver-blind regions.} Every receiver-ray defense keeps what the receiver cannot see. The
receiver-blind spoof was realized on \RealizedSpoofBlind{} frames; \BlindRealizedLowRay{} of them landed where the
receiver had fewer than three rays (or on itself), and \BlindRealizedKnownHit{} touched a KNOWN unit. There, B-RAY's $\Delta$AP is
\dGlobSpoofBlindBRAY\pts{} and R1's \dGlobSpoofBlindRONE\pts{} against an attack loss of \LossGlobSpoofBlind\pts{} (global-ranking AP). Even the visibility-limited attacker oracle
bounds recovery at \VisOracleRecSpoofBlind{} (frame-order; the unconstrained oracle reaches \OracleRecSpoofBlind).
R1 likewise cannot verify a removal in a region the receiver cannot see. Closing this gap needs evidence other
than the receiver's own rays, such as other benign senders' scans, which brings back the trust problem.

\textbf{Adaptive attackers.} Stealth PGD shows how cheaply a defense that only looks at feature statistics is
bypassed. Our attacks do not adapt to R1 or B-RAY: an attacker who places fakes where the rays are ambiguous
(fewer than four traversing rays) or that the receiver cannot see is not stopped. The attack levels were chosen
on exposed development data, and the strong levels after seeing results there.

\textbf{Single attacker.} The attacker is always sender~1, alone. Two colluding senders could each confirm the
other's fake; R1's per-sender counterfactual removes one sender at a time and would miss it.

\textbf{Simulation.} OPV2V is CARLA simulation~\cite{dosovitskiy2017carla}. The Culver City run tests transfer to an unseen
town layout under the same simulated sensor, not to real sensors, real traffic or real attacks. Real LiDAR misses dark or glass surfaces (more
UNKNOWN) and returns from vegetation or spray (false support). The receiver's sensor is assumed honest; physical
spoofing~\cite{cao2019advlidar} would break that.

\textbf{Compute.} Dense R1 scales with the number of senders and exceeds the receiver's own perception time at
$n\ge 4$ on our CPU.

\textbf{No fresh data for tuning.} R1 has no threshold, but the primary was selected and the stealth attacks
designed on block~H after it was exposed. The test was run once; its results cannot be used to tune anything
further without new data.

\textbf{Statistics.} The bootstrap $p$ of Eq.~\eqref{eq:p} is the bootstrap mass at or below zero, not a
null-calibrated test, and percentile intervals over 15 unequal clusters may under-cover. Attacks that are not
realized and $n=1$ frames dilute every all-frame $\Delta$AP equally.

\textbf{Agent count.} The test effects shrink with $n$: under frame-order AP, B-RAY's mean gain falls from
\ByNTwoBRAY\pts{} at $n=2$ to \ByNFourPlusBRAY\pts{} at $n\ge 4$, and R1's from \ByNTwoRONE{} to \ByNFourPlusRONE\pts{}
(10-frame CIs; $n\ge4$ covers \ByNFourPlusScen{} scenarios).

%======================================================================
\section{Conclusion and Future Work}
%======================================================================
In a pre-registered, one-time test, a receiver-only box-level free-space filter (B-RAY) passed its
pre-registered rule narrowly; R1, a tile-level counterfactual verified by the receiver's own rays, was the only
defense positive in every condition under global-ranking AP and the only one that recovered removal attacks.
A norm check failed against stealthy attacks, and no receiver-ray method helped in receiver-blind regions.
Which of R1 and B-RAY looks better depends on the AP definition, so CP papers should report both.
On the unseen Culver City town (simulated sensor; secondary), the signs of these effects held, but B-RAY's
global-ranking gain was not significant on four scenarios.

Three directions follow. (i) A hybrid that uses B-RAY's box filter for added objects and only R1's REMOVE test
for removals; our ablation suggests the REMOVE test carries the removal recovery, but the hybrid is untested.
(ii) Validation on real-sensor data never touched by method design, such as
V2V4Real~\cite{xu2023v2v4real}; Culver City covers only a simulated domain shift. (iii) Per-frame checkpointing of the test stream, which currently writes
results per completed scenario.
